summary: Generalizes the pseudowire Associated Channel Header so a control channel can be attached to MPLS label switched paths and MPLS sections, not just pseudowires. It also defines how to signal the presence of the header in the label stack, which helps with operations and management messages.

eli5.summary: Besides the packages on a delivery route, you sometimes want a small side channel for the workers to chat. This sets up that side channel along the route.

subtitle: How MPLS paths and links get a built-in side channel for maintenance messages, flagged by reserved label 13.

tldr.problem: Operators need in-band maintenance tools such as fault detection and protection switching that work the same way on pseudowires, label switched paths and MPLS sections, but the associated channel header existed only for pseudowires.
tldr.mechanism: The pseudowire Associated Channel Header (ACH) is generalized to LSPs and sections, and a reserved label, the G-ACh Label (GAL), signals that an ACH follows the bottom of the label stack.
tldr.outcome: The document defines only the encapsulation. Channel types, signaling and the OAM functions themselves are left to other documents. RFC 5586 is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by several RFCs.

today: RFC 5586 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3032, RFC 4385 and RFC 5085, and it has itself been updated by RFC 6423, RFC 7026, RFC 7214 and RFC 7274. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Generic Associated Channel
sections.content:
Operators need Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) tools for fault detection, diagnostics and maintenance on pseudowires (PWs) and Label Switched Paths (LSPs). The RFC lists examples such as performance monitoring, automatic protection switching, and support for management and signaling communication channels.

These tools MUST work in essentially the same way on MPLS PWs, LSPs and MPLS Sections. They MUST also run in-band, so they do not depend on packet network routing or on user traffic, and MUST NOT depend on dynamic control plane functions.

Pseudowire VCCV (RFC 5085) already used an Associated Channel Header for a control channel between PW endpoints. RFC 5586 generalizes that into the Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) for sections, LSPs and PWs. It does not define how the channel is signaled or negotiated, does not define the OAM functions, and does not deprecate existing MPLS and PW OAM mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Network workers need a way to check that a route is healthy without bothering the parcels. This gives every kind of route the same small side lane for those checks.

sections.title: The Associated Channel Header
sections.content:
The ACH is a single 32-bit word. Its first nibble is set to 0001 to say that a control channel is associated with a PW, LSP or Section. The Version field is set to 0, as specified in RFC 4385. Bits 8 to 15 are reserved: they MUST be set to 0 and ignored on reception. Bits 16 to 31 carry the Channel Type, in network byte order.

The Channel Type says what is carried: IPv4 or IPv6 if IP demultiplexing is used, or the specific protocol when IP is not used. Each document that defines a protocol relying on the ACH MUST also specify its Channel Type value. For PWs, the PWE3 control word MUST be present in the encapsulation of user packets when the ACH is used. The G-ACh MUST NOT be used to transport user traffic.
sections.eli5: The header is a small label on each note that says what kind of note it is, like writing 'repair report' on an envelope.

sections.title: Optional ACH TLVs
sections.content:
Some channel types need extra context, for example to name the source or intended destination of a message. For this the RFC defines ACH TLVs. They are allowed only if the Channel Type definition explicitly says that TLVs MAY precede the message. If it does, an ACH TLV Header MUST follow the ACH. If a packet carries no TLVs, the header is still present with its length field set to zero. If the Channel Type does not allow TLVs, the ACH TLV Header MUST NOT be used.

The ACH TLV Header has a 16-bit Length (the total octets of all TLVs and sub-TLVs that follow) and a 16-bit Reserved field set to zero. Each TLV has a 16-bit Type, a 16-bit Length counting the octets of the Value, and then the Value, which MAY contain sub-TLVs. No padding is required.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a note needs a sticky label such as 'from here, to there'. These labels are optional, and the note type must say they are allowed.

sections.title: The G-ACh Label and How It Is Used
sections.content:
On an LSP or Section there is no pseudowire to tell a router that a packet is a control message, so RFC 5586 uses a reserved label from RFC 3032, the G-ACh Label (GAL). IANA assigned the value 13. The GAL flags the packet as a G-ACh packet and indicates that the ACH appears immediately after the bottom of the label stack. It MUST only be used where both apply.

In MPLS-TP the GAL MUST be used on LSPs, Concatenated Segments and Sections, MUST NOT be used with PWs, and MUST always be at the bottom of the stack (S bit set to 1). The GAL MUST NOT appear in the stack for normal user packets, MUST NOT appear more than once, and a node MUST NOT forward a G-ACh packet onward based on the GAL.

To send on an LSP, the ingress LER builds the G-ACh message, optionally prepends an ACH TLV Header and TLVs, adds the ACH, pushes a GAL entry and then the LSP label. The GAL TTL MUST be set to at least 1, and its value and the TC field are application specific. Intermediate LSRs MUST NOT modify the message, ACH or GAL. The targeted destination SHOULD pass the whole packet to the right processing entity. On a Section, the GAL may be the only label in the stack, giving a channel across one link between two LSRs.
sections.eli5: A special flag, label number 13, is stuck on a packet to say 'this is a maintenance note, not a parcel'. Only the right person at the end of the route reads it.

sections.title: Relationship to Older Alerts and Handling Unknown Packets
sections.content:
Older MPLS OAM (RFC 4379 and BFD for MPLS) uses TTL expiration or an IP destination in the range 127.0.0.0/8 for IPv4. These stay the default way to identify OAM packets that are inside IP. The GAL mechanism is RECOMMENDED when IP-based mechanisms are not available, as in MPLS-TP, and MAY be used in addition.

RFC 3429 already assigned the OAM Alert Label, value 14. A new label was needed because G-ACh messages sit behind the ACH after the bottom of the stack, the set of maintenance functions is wider, and existing deployments make it impossible to change label 14. The RFC RECOMMENDS that no further OAM extensions based on label 14 be developed.

A node MUST discard an associated channel packet whose labels are all popped if it cannot process the Channel Type, has not agreed to process it, receives an experimental channel type that is locally disabled, finds a first nibble other than 0001 after a GAL, or does not recognize the ACH version. It MAY also count the error or send an SNMP notification.
sections.eli5: Old notes used a different flag, label 14, and people still rely on it, so this adds a new flag instead. If a worker gets a note type they do not understand, they throw it away.

sections.title: Security and Congestion
sections.content: The security considerations for the associated control channel are those of RFC 4385. RFC 5085 provides data plane security considerations, and these also apply to a G-ACh whether the alert uses a GAL or only an ACH. Any further security considerations MUST be described in the relevant channel type specification. For congestion, the considerations in RFC 5085 apply.
sections.eli5: The safety rules come from earlier documents, and each new kind of note must add its own rules.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Experimental Code Points
sections.content:
IANA allocated label value 13 for the GAL. Channel Types come from the PW Associated Channel Type registry. Its policy was changed so that values 0 to 32751 are allocated by IETF Review, while values 32760 to 32767 are Experimental. Experimental code points MUST follow RFC 3692, functions using them MUST be disabled by default, and the Channel Type used MUST be configurable.

The registry gained a column saying whether an ACH TLV header follows. The two existing entries are 0x21 (ACH carries an IPv4 packet) and 0x57 (ACH carries an IPv6 packet), and both have no TLV header. A new ACH TLV Registry was created with IETF Review and no initial entries.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of note types. A few spots are set aside for experiments, and anything experimental must be off until someone turns it on.

fields.name: First nibble
fields.desc: Set to 0001 for a control channel on a PW, LSP or Section.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 and ignored on reception.

fields.name: Channel Type
fields.desc: What protocol or function the channel carries.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets of all TLVs and sub-TLVs that follow; zero means none.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero on transmission and ignored on reception.
